full_judgment:
That the present petitioner as plaintiff filed a suit being Title Suit No. 297 of 1989 before the 2nd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka against the Opposite Parties for permanent injunction restraining the defendant-opposite parties from carrying on any activities of the Trade Union directly or indirectly either by themselves or through their representatives. That immediately after filing the suit, the plaintiff-petitioner filed an application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for temporary injunction. It is stated in that application for temporary injunction that the plaintiff No. 2 is the President of Titas Gas Union having registration No. B-1193 and the other plaintiffs are members of the said Trade Union. It is asserted in the said petition that the plaintiff Trade Union represents the General members of the Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Ltd. and acts as the bargaining agent under the provisions of Industrial Relations Ordinance 1969. That the defendants 1 and 2 and their associates were also the members of the plaintiffs. Trade Union and they paid their subscriptions up to the month of October, 1989 and they never resigned from the plaintiffs Trade Union. That on 18.10.89 the defendants 1 and 2 by showing fake list of members in the name of the defendant No. 3, Trade Union, obtained the Registration of the Trade Union most illegally. It is asserted that the said Union was formed illegally and the plaintiffs Union filed Title Suit No. 221 of 1986 in Court of Assistant Judge, 4th Court Dhaka and obtained an order of status-quo on 13.5.87. That order of status quo was subsequently vacated by the learned Judge and no appeal was filed thereto. 

 3. The learned Assistant Judge on perusal of the application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 CPC issued show-cause notice upon the defendants and granted ad interim order of injunction on 14.11.89. The defendants opposite parties thus being aggrieved preferred an Appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 276 of 1989 before the learned District Judge and the learned District Judge admitted the appeal and stayed the operation of the order of ad interim injunction granted by the Assistant Judge on 14.11.89. Thus being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the order passed by the learned District Judge, the plaintiff petitioners have filed this Revisional Application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present rule. 

 4. Mr. SR Pal, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners, submits that the order of the learned District Judge dated 18.11.89 staying the operation of the order dated 14.11.89 passed by the Assistant Judge is highly illegal and as such the same is not sustainable in law. Mr. Pal argues that the defendants Trade Union being established collusively on practising fraud upon the Registrar and as such the said registration is illegal and the defendants opposite parties are required under law to be restrained by an order of injunction from carrying on with their activities of the Trade Union. The learned District Judge has committed a serious error of law in staying the operation of the order of stay granted by the Assistant Judge, Dhaka dated 14.11.89. Mr. Pal also argues that the suit as filed by the plaintiff-petitioners is perfectly maintainable and as such the relief sought for should be granted in order that the plaintiffs legal right might be protected. 

 5. Mr. M. Nurullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-opposite parties, on the other hand, argues that the defendants out of their own free accord formed the Trade Union and obtained the registration after complying with the legal formalities and as such they are free to carry on their activities unfettered and the learned Assistant Judge has no right or power under law to restrain them from carrying on such activities. Mr. Nurullah argues that the plaintiff petitioners also filed a suit against the granting of registration (in favour of the defendants Trade Union) before the 4th Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka and the learned Subordinate Judge summarily rejected the prayer for injunction with the observation that the defendant opposite parties have formed the Trade Union legally and as such have a right to carry on with the activities of the Trade Union in accordance with law. That order of the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka is still in force as the plaintiffs had preferred no appeal or revision thereto before the higher Court. Mr. Nurullah also argues that suppression of this material fact in the petition for injunction will disentitle the plaintiffs from getting any relief under the discretionary power of the Court. 

 6. The defendant-opposite parties in this rule have appeared and filed an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the statements made by the plaintiff-petitioner in the petition on material particulars. 

 9. Mr. Pal argues that the liability of the plaintiffs to exercise their activities as members of the Trade Union was there in existence but the statute namely, the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 has only regulated the same. Therefore the plaintiffs have an election to choose either the common law remedy or the remedy provided by the statute. And therefore, the suit as well as the petition for injunction both are maintainable in law. Mr. Pal argues that for the purpose of carrying on the activities of the Trade Union, the registration of the Trade Union is necessary. To challenge the granting of the registration of the union before the Civil Court is perfectly maintainable as the activities thereof are rooted in the common law. 

 "Injunction to restrain repetition or continuance of breach-(1) In any suit for restraining the defendant from committing a breach of contract or other injury of any kind, whether compensation is claimed in the suit or not, the plaintiff may, at any time after the commencement of the suit, and either before or after judgment, apply to the Court for a temporary injunction to restrain the defendant from committing the breach of contract or injury complained of, or any breach of contract or injury of a like kind arising out of the same contract or relating to the same property or right". 

 15. The plaintiff must set out the right in his plaint so claimed in the suit and also must show that the defendants threaten or repeat or continue to repeat causing injury to the right claimed by the plaintiff petitioner in his petition under Order 39 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 (i) has a prima facie case or a legal right that in order to protect that case, the legal right, he needs an order from the Court to protect the same that the injury complained of must be arising from the species of injury known as "irreparable" injury separated from the injury which may be compensated by money. 

 Mere making out a prima facie case will not entitle an applicant to have an order of injunction. The question of irreparable injury and balance of convenience should also be considered along with making out of a prima facie case. 

 When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiffs right to, or enjoyment of, property, the Court may grant a perpetual in-junction in the following cases (namely)— 

 (a) whether the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; 

 21. The obligation as referred to under section 54 of the Specific Relief Act must exist in favour of the plaintiff and that the defendants arc threatening to commit breach of such obligation standing in favour of the plaintiff. In the instant case the facts disclosed are as such that the plaintiffs are members of a registered Trade Union under the law. That the defendant opposite parties have also formed an independent Trade Union and that Union has duly been registered under the law. In the face of two separate entities recognised under the law, neither the plaintiff nor the defendants has any legal obligation as against the other and committing any breach of the legal right does not arise at all and as such neither party is to be prevented by an order of injunction so that their activities may be restrained. The legal right as claimed by the plaintiff under the cover of registration of their Trade Union is similarly being enjoyed by the defendants opposite parties under the cover of valid registration of their Trade Union. Under such circumstances of the case, it cannot be said either Trade Union is under any obligation and that being so neither party should be restrained by any order of injunction. In facts and circumstances of the case no injunction lies. It is now well settled that in order to get an order of injunction from any court, the applicant must satisfy the court that he has a prima facie case and further that there is an obligation in his favour which the defendant owes but threatens to commit breach of such obligation and that unless he gets an order of injunction, his legal right will be frustrated and that the injury would be irreparable if no such order of injunction is granted. So the prima facie case the plaintiffs assert that their Trade Union is a recognised one and that the Trade Union of the defendants is vague cannot be accepted in view of the fact that the Trade Union of the defendants is also registered and that the remedy available to the plaintiff for cancellation of the registration of the defendants Trade Union has not been availed of before the competent forum. The fact is that both the plaintiffs and the defendants are two separate Trade Unions under the cover of law and hence I find no obligation exists in favour of the plaintiff to call for any interference from this Court. So the plaintiffs petitioners have failed to prove any prima facie case in their favour. Secondly, as to the balance of convenience and in-convenience in the matter before me I find that the defendants Trade Union being legally constituted by the valid law of the land and they have a right to carry on with their activities and if the Court passes an order of injunction restraining them that will put them to serious inconvenience and as such it is to be held that balance of convenience is in favour of the defendants and not in favour of the plaintiffs. I have already found that both the plaintiffs and the defendants are members of different Trade Unions having the Unions registered and one cannot restrain the other from carrying on with activities of the Trade Union. Court must vindicate or protect legal right and further keep watch so that such right is not in any way fettered. It must not create any hindrance or impediment in the exercise of such right and no order of injunction is to be issued restraining the exercise of a legal right. Therefore, the order passed by the learned District Judge in staying the operation of the order passed by the Assistant Judge does not appear to suffer from any infirmity or illegality. I find that the order of the learned District Judge is sustainable in law and there is nothing to interfere with.
